tracks.title: The graveyard of session scripts
tracks.text: Lesson 03 point 4 — promotion. A sub-lesson, under toolkit. [curious] Picture the graveyard of session scripts. An agent, or you, writes a useful little program mid-session — a slug-maker, a CSV cleaner, a parser that finally tames some ragged scraper output. It works. And then, in nearly every stack ever built… that's where it dies. A file in a scratch directory. Copy-pasted into the next project. Drifting out of true a little more every time someone touches it. The gap between code that worked once here… and a tool everyone can install… is normally a cliff. A repo. A build pipeline. A registry account. An afternoon. [sighs] So most one-off tools never make the climb. This lesson is about turning that cliff into a ladder — three rungs, two commands.

tracks.title: The ladder
tracks.text: The ladder. Here's the definition. Promotion is the lifecycle ladder a tool climbs — session… to workspace… to registry. And these three rungs are named verbatim in the engine. Picture three steps. First, the session rung — a command called build-inline compiles your source in the sandbox and registers it live. No manifest. No project. Second, the workspace rung — a command called promote writes a real toolkit directory… source plus a generated manifest… that rebuilds forever. Third, the registry rung — the toolkit is just a workbook, so one call stores it and another installs it on a different machine. [excited] Same source the whole way up. What changes at each rung is only how durable the tool is… and how far it can travel.

tracks.title: Rung one — no manifest ceremony
tracks.text: Rung one — no manifest ceremony. One command turns a source file into a live, callable tool. You type — wbx toolkit build-inline, slug, js, slug dot js. And the engine answers back, word for word — built and registered command slug, javascript… arrow… build slash commands slash, a long hash, dot wasm. Run it via the Dock — run-command slug. No project to scaffold. No manifest to write. The pipeline is exactly four stages. First… write. Second… build in the sandbox. Third… content-address. Fourth… register. Six languages have an inline lane — rust, C, zig, javascript, typescript, and go. And the whole build runs entirely inside the wasm sandbox… no native toolchain… no host escape… because the compiler is itself wasm. [curious] Now picture that pipeline as a graph. The source file flows into the sandbox build. The build flows into the content-address step — a sha256 of the wasm bytes. The content-address step does two things — it registers the binding in memory… and it parks the bytes at build slash commands slash, that hash, dot wasm. And here's the load-bearing part. Identical source compiles to identical wasm… which produces an identical hash… which lands at the same path. So rebuilds are idempotent, by construction. The registry is guarded too — a built command's path must canonicalize inside the commands directory, the dynamic table is capped at four thousand and ninety-six entries against denial-of-service, and the four built-ins are merged into lookup last… so a poisoned key can never shadow a real one.

tracks.title: What session means
tracks.text: Now the precise part — what session actually means. This is a depth rung… skippable. Rung one is called the session rung because the binding is ephemeral. But be precise about which part dies. The engine's own words — a session command is built into persistent-term, gone when the Instance dies. And yet the compiled artifact is content-addressed on disk… so those bytes persist. What's ephemeral is the binding — the name pointing at the bytes — not the bytes themselves. Hold two rows side by side. First row — the binding, the mapping of slug to this wasm. It lives in memory. Does it survive the Instance dying? No… gone with the Instance. Second row — the artifact, the wasm bytes. It lives content-addressed on disk. Does it survive? Yes… never deleted. [excited] So the verdict is simple — the work isn't lost… the wiring is. And the engine softens even that. A small registry dot json manifest in the commands directory lets a boot-time reload re-register the built commands from their cached artifacts. The bytes were already on disk… the manifest just remembers which names pointed where. And one more thing falls out of never deleting the bytes — hot-swap. Re-register a name and the binding replaces live, no restart. In-flight calls finish on the old bytes… because the old file still exists. Replacing a tool never yanks the rug out from under a call already running on it.

tracks.title: Rung two — promote
tracks.text: Rung two — promote. The second command materializes the session command as a real, source-owned toolkit directory. You type — wbx toolkit promote, slug, js, slug dot js. And it answers — promoted session command, arrow, workspace toolkit slug at toolkits slash slug. Build it… wb toolkit build slug. Then it packs into a workbook and installs elsewhere. Before it writes anything, promote runs four guards in order. First… the name can't be a reserved built-in. Second… it must match the allowed character pattern. Third… the language must be one of the six. Fourth… the source file must exist. Trip a guard and you get a clean refusal. Try to promote a tool named grep, and it says — cannot promote, grep is a reserved built-in command name. [curious] And here's the key move — promote scaffolds, it does not build. Picture the rust case on disk afterward. A folder, toolkits slash slug. Inside it… manifest dot org, the generated spec. A Cargo dot toml, synthesized for you, naming the package slug, version zero point one point zero. A src slash main dot rs… which is your source, verbatim. And a skills slash overview dot org… a skill stub with a verification checklist. The manifest carries the keys that make it real — exec command, trust first-party, CLI-bin slug, build-lang rust, build-source path dot, arg-mode argv, status experimental. And a headline — star, slug, colon toolkit colon. That tag is not decoration… it's what makes the tool discoverable by a tags-toolkit query, the same way every other toolkit is found.

tracks.title: Org owns the spec, wasm owns the artifact
tracks.text: Org owns the spec… wasm owns the artifact. This is the rung's thesis, and the engine states it plainly — promotion persists the source, rebuildable… not just the compiled bytes. Why does that matter? A directory of compiled bytes rots the moment the compiler moves. A directory of source plus a declarative manifest can be rebuilt forever… into the identical artifact. [excited] Picture the rebuild as a chain. On the left… the manifest, declaring build-lang rust, build-source path dot, CLI-bin slug. That feeds the build directory — source main dot rs, plus the Cargo dot toml. That feeds the compile, in the sandbox. That feeds the content-address — sha256 of the wasm. And on the right… the same sha as the session build. Read it as a story — the manifest is the recipe, the wasm is the dish, and the recipe always cooks the same dish. Same source… same compiler… same hash… same path. The deterministic rebuild meets the session build at the very same artifact. And the trust line is what makes sharing possible — trust stays first-party, yours. A third-party consumer grants its own caps on install. Your manifest says trust first-party because it's yours. When someone else installs it… they decide what it's allowed to touch. Nobody inherits your grants.

tracks.title: Per-language layouts
tracks.text: Per-language layouts. Another depth rung… skippable. Here's a small puzzle — why does rust get a build-source of path dot, and a synthesized Cargo dot toml… while everyone else gets path src? Because the rust build directory wants source main dot rs with the Cargo dot toml beside it at the toolkit root. The other languages just want their entry file directly under the folder handed to the compiler. Picture the table, six rows. Rust… build-source path dot, entry source main dot rs, plus that synthesized Cargo file. C… path src, entry source main dot c, no extras. Zig… path src, source main dot zig. Go… path src, source main dot go. Javascript… path src, source index dot js. Typescript… path src, source index dot ts. [curious] The verdict in one line — rust is the exception that needs a manifest file inside the build directory, so it gets path dot plus a Cargo file. The other five just need their entry under a source folder, so they get path src and nothing extra. The split isn't arbitrary… it's the build directory each compiler expects, encoded once in the layout table instead of remembered five times.

tracks.title: Rung three — a toolkit is a workbook
tracks.text: Rung three — a toolkit is a workbook. This is where the tool leaves your machine. And here's the move that makes it cheap — there is no separate toolkit package format. A toolkit is a workbook. Everything is reuse — publishing is store, searching is search, signing is the bundle's ship step, sharing rides the same member path workbooks already use. [excited] Picture the journey as a sequence between two machines. Nexus A, the publisher, calls store — it packs the workbook, and each command ships as a name dot wasm part. The result lands on the storage backend — local, S3, or R2 — as a slug dot wbundle, tenant-scoped, auto-indexed for search. Then Nexus B, the installer, fetches that blob. And before anything registers, two gates fire. First gate — the sha pin. The sha256 of the blob must match. Second gate — the signature check, optional, off by default for first-party local installs. Only then does Nexus B unpack and register each wasm part… capped by its own Policy. And the result comes back — okay, commands slug. The registered commands land under the same ceiling as everything else… which the engine says in five words — installing never widens caps. And that sentence is the bridge to the security story… because the same thing is true of authoring.

tracks.title: The capability ceiling
tracks.text: The capability ceiling. [curious] Self-authoring sounds like the start of an incident report. Agents writing and running their own tools? The invariant that makes it safe is structural… not policed. The Dock imports an Instance can see are built from its Policy capabilities, by construction. The host provides only the imports the Policy grants. So a component that tries to import a capability it wasn't granted… simply fails to instantiate. Run-command is one of those imports — it exists only if the commands cap is granted. So authoring a tool never grants the tool anything. A built command runs through the very same gate as every other command. An ungranted capability is un-importable… therefore un-callable. Picture the four real Policy profiles. First, minimal — sixty-four mebibytes, a five-second timeout… it can build and run, but the tool gets nothing the profile didn't grant. Second, network — one hundred and twenty-eight mebibytes, thirty seconds, and it adds network. Third, posix — two hundred and fifty-six mebibytes, sixty seconds, the widest standard profile. And fourth, compute — sixty-four mebibytes, five seconds… and caps of vfs only. No commands at all. [excited] And there's the whole security story in one example. An Instance on compute can't even call a command it authored… because run-command was never imported. An Instance on minimal can build and run slug… but slug gets no network, no model access, nothing minimal didn't already hand it. The tool can never exceed the granted set… no matter who wrote it. Trust shapes one more thing — the isolation tier. Trust is recorded at build, defaulting to first-party, and third-party commands run isolated on a separate virtual machine. The build gate refuses third-party toolkits with bad provenance… and refuses any binary name that would shadow a reserved one. And every run-command call appends a step to the steps log — the tool name, exit code, duration, timestamp. The whole episode is on the record.

tracks.title: Scaffold, not a publish button
tracks.text: Now the honest part — scaffold, not a publish button. Promote is a scaffold… not a publish button. The generated skill stub is deliberately minimal — a when-to-use, a one-line workflow, two checkboxes — and it says so. Extend the skill as the toolkit grows. The manual layer the parent lesson celebrates… still has to be written by someone. Promotion gives you the skeleton, not the muscle. And the lanes have edges, so let's name them. First… six languages, not all of them. Second… inline crates-io dependencies are rust-only on the build-inline lane, while javascript and typescript take npm deps through a synthesized package file — the dependency story isn't uniform across the six. Third… the session rung is ephemeral by design. The binding is gone when the Instance dies, and while the bytes and a reload manifest soften that, the rung is a workbench, not a vault. And fourth… the reserved names. You can't call your tool grep, jq, upper, or wbox — the built-ins win those names, always. A toolkit comes out the door marked status experimental, because that's honestly what a freshly promoted session command is. None of this is software that runs itself… it's a ladder that makes the climb cheap, with a human deciding what's worth climbing.

tracks.title: Questions people actually ask
tracks.text: Quick fire. [curious] Can my agent really do this unattended? Yes… and it's capped the whole time. It can write a file, build-inline it live, and promote it — no human in the loop. What it can't do is grant itself anything. What if I promote the same name twice? Promote writes into a named directory, so a second promote targets the same path. Treat it as a scaffold you re-run… copy grown work aside first. Why can't I name it grep? Because grep is a reserved built-in… along with jq, upper, and wbox, and the built-ins win lookup so a dynamic name can never shadow them. Do I have to promote, or can I live on build-inline? You can live on build-inline — rung one is a complete tool for the life of the Instance, and the reload manifest brings it back at boot. Promote when you want it source-owned, rebuildable, packable, and discoverable. Does the consumer get my capabilities? No. Trust stays first-party, yours. They grant their own caps on install… installing never widens caps. And will my rebuilt tool have the same hash? By the content-addressing rule it should — same source, same compiler, same sha, same path. [chuckles] We say should rather than always, on purpose… the determinism follows from the design, and that's the principle we stand behind, not a promise we'll overstate.

tracks.title: Back up to the toolkit
tracks.text: So that's promotion. One source file… climbing three rungs of durability. Session, where build-inline registers it live. Workspace, where promote materializes a source-owned, rebuildable toolkit. And registry, where store and install ship it to another machine. Org owns the spec… wasm owns the artifact… and the invariant underneath it all — authoring a tool never grants the tool anything. [curious] The way back up is short. This is the rung after the toolkit lesson's one sentence about it — so if you want the anatomy, the manual, and the wasm bet that makes the whole thing possible… that's the parent lesson, toolkit. Start there… and everything you heard here hangs off it.
